name: Biritch
description: Biritch, or Russian Whist, is the earliest known form of Bridge â€” the game that the word 'Bridge' originally referred to before Auction Bridge and Contract Bridge evolved from it. It is a 4-player partnership trick-taking game using a standard 52-card deck. Unlike Whist, no trump is turned up; instead the dealer (or dealer's partner) declares trumps or calls 'biritch' (no-trump). The dealer's partner's hand is then exposed as a 'Dummy', played by the dealer â€” the defining innovation that would eventually lead to modern Contract Bridge.

history.origins: The game was played in the Russian colony at Constantinople (Istanbul) during the 1880s. John Collinson, a British railway engineer working in Turkey between 1880â€“1884, learned the game there and introduced it to friends in England. He published a small booklet titled 'Biritch, or Russian Whist' on 9 July 1886, registered at Stationers' Hall â€” the earliest known document describing any form of Bridge.
timeline: 1880-1884: John Collinson plays Biritch in the Russian colony at Constantinople.
1886: Collinson publishes 'Biritch, or Russian Whist' â€” the first bridge rules ever printed.
1906: Collinson writes to The Saturday Review confirming the game's origins.
1890s-1920s: Evolves into Auction Bridge (players bid for the right to name trumps).
1925: Harold Vanderbilt develops Contract Bridge from Auction Bridge.
1940-41: One of the four known surviving copies is destroyed in the London Blitz.
history.cultural: Biritch represents the missing link between Whist (no trump declaration, no dummy) and modern Bridge. The word 'bridge' likely derives from 'biritch', though the etymology remains debated by scholars. The game's transmission from the Russian community in Constantinople via a British engineer embodies the cosmopolitan card-game culture of the 19th-century Ottoman Empire.
history.evolution: Biritch introduced two revolutionary concepts to the Whist family: (1) the dealer declares trumps rather than turning a card, and (2) the partner's hand is exposed as 'Dummy.' These innovations laid the foundation for all subsequent Bridge variants. Only three copies of the original 1886 booklet survive (Bodleian Library Oxford, Cambridge University Library, Public Record Office London).

setup.players: 4 players in fixed partnerships, seated opposite each other. Cutting for partners, shuffling, and dealing are the same as at Short Whist.
setup.deck: Standard 52-card deck. Card ranking as at Whist: A (high), K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2.
setup.dealing: 13 cards dealt to each player. Unlike Whist, NO card is turned up for trumps.

rules.objective: Win tricks with your partnership. The first side to score 30 points in play wins a game. Best of three games (a rubber) wins the rubber.
rules.gameplay: Four players in fixed partnerships, as at short whist. No card is turned for trumps. After the deal the dealer may declare a suit for trumps or say pass, in which case the partner must declare. The declarer may instead say biritch (no trumps). After declaration either adversary may say contre (doubles trick values); the dealer side may say sur contre (quadruples), and doubling may continue until one side stops. The player to the left of the dealer leads. The dealer's partner then exposes all cards as Dummy, played by the dealer; Dummy may not suggest plays. Revokes and misdeals as at short whist. A game is 30 points in play; honours do not count toward the game. Best of three games wins the rubber.
keyRules: Dealer (or partner) declares trumps â€” no card turned up. Revolutionary departure from Whist.
'Biritch' = no-trump declaration. The origin of the word 'Bridge.'
Dummy hand is exposed and played by the dealer.
30 points wins a game. Best of 3 games wins the rubber.
Honours score separately and do not affect games.

strategy.basic: Standard Whist principles apply: lead from your longest suit, support partner's leads, save trumps for capturing high cards. The Dummy exposure gives the declaring side a major information advantage.
strategy.intermediate: Trump declaration strategy: with a strong suit of 5+ cards, declare that suit. With balanced strength and high cards across suits, declare 'biritch' (no-trump) to maximise the value of standalone Aces and Kings.
strategy.advanced: Contreing: challenge the opponents' declaration if you hold strong trumps or length in their declared suit. The risk/reward of contre vs. sur-contre adds a psychological dimension absent from regular Whist. Reading the Dummy: after the Dummy is exposed, the lead player can see 26 of 52 cards â€” use this to plan a precise line of attack.
tips: The exposed Dummy gives the declaring side a huge advantage â€” use it to finesse and promote intermediate cards.
Preserve your trumps when defending: don't waste them on tricks the declaring side would win anyway.
Honour scoring is separate from game scoring â€” don't chase honours at the expense of trick-winning.

variations.name: Auction Bridge (Successor)
variations.description: Evolved from Biritch in the 1900s. All four players bid competitively for the right to name trumps, replacing fixed dealer declaration.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Describes Auction Bridge as a historical successor only; specific engine overrides are not modeled yet.

variations.name: Contract Bridge (Modern Successor)
variations.description: Developed by Harold Vanderbilt in 1925. Only tricks bid and won count toward game; overtricks score separately. The dominant form of Bridge today.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Describes Contract Bridge as a later successor; detailed engine overrides will be added in its own game entry.

scoring.description: Odd tricks (above 6) count toward game score. 30 points = one game. Best 2 of 3 games = rubber. Honours scored separately.
scoring.winCondition: First side to win 2 games wins the rubber.

synthesis.shortDescription: The ancestor of all Bridge games, first documented in 1886 by a British engineer who learned it from the Russian colony in Constantinople. The dealer declares trumps (or 'biritch' for no-trump), the partner's hand is exposed as Dummy, and the race to 30 points begins. Only three copies of the original rules survive.
